chapter.name: Nature's Treasures
chapter.blurb: Nature provides essential resources: air (a gas mixture, mainly nitrogen and oxygen), water (mostly saline, with limited usable freshwater needing conservation), energy from the Sun (the ultimate source of all energy, direct and via solar panels), forests and soil/rocks/minerals, and fossil fuels (petroleum, natural gas, coal). Natural resources are classified as renewable (air, water, forests) or non-renewable (minerals, soil, rocks, coal, petroleum, natural gas), distinct from human-made resources.

scope_in.item: Air is a mixture of gases surrounding the Earth: nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), argon/carbon dioxide/other gases (1%); oxygen is needed for survival; moving air is called wind, used in windmills for flour mills, water pumping and electricity generation

Water's uses (drinking, cooking, growing crops, industry); most of Earth's water is saline (oceans/seas); freshwater sources are ice/snow, rivers/lakes and groundwater, of which only a small accessible fraction is usable; water conservation, water pollution, and rainwater harvesting (including traditional stepwells: Bawadi in Rajasthan, Vav in Gujarat)

The Sun as the main source of energy on Earth; plants make food using sunlight, and this energy passes to animals that eat plants; direct uses of solar energy: solar panels (electricity), solar cookers, solar water heaters, and drying food/clothes
Forests: large areas of dense plant growth, home to wild animals, supporting biodiversity; deforestation and slow forest regeneration; the Chipko movement as an Indian forest-protection effort

Soil formed by disintegration of rocks by the Sun, water and living organisms over a very long time; roots hold soil in place; decaying leaves enrich soil with nutrients (natural recycling); earthworms loosen and turn soil; rocks used for construction/roofing/tools; rocks are made of minerals, from which metals (aluminium, gold, copper, iron) are extracted; minerals used in electronics (e.g. a mobile phone contains about a dozen minerals)

Fossil fuels -- petroleum (giving petrol, diesel, kerosene), natural gas (cooking, electricity, CNG for vehicles), and coal (mainly electricity) -- formed from remains of microorganisms and plants buried underground over millions of years; limited supply; burning them causes air pollution; LPG/natural gas have gradually replaced coal/wood/dung cakes as domestic fuels

Natural resources (from nature) versus human-made resources (created by humans); renewable resources (renewed/replenished within a reasonable time, e.g. air, water, forests) versus non-renewable resources (limited, not replenished in reasonable time, e.g. minerals, soil, rocks, coal, petroleum, natural gas)

concepts.name: Air: composition and importance
concepts.description: Air is a mixture of gases surrounding the Earth -- mostly nitrogen and oxygen -- essential for survival, with moving air called wind.
concepts.idea: Air is a mixture of gases that surrounds the Earth; it is essential for the survival of living beings, mainly because of the oxygen it contains.
concepts.rule: Air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% argon/carbon dioxide/other gases; moving air is called wind, ranging from a gentle breeze to a fast storm.
concepts.example: Holding your breath quickly becomes uncomfortable because the body needs continuous oxygen; a firki or a windmill's wings turn because of wind, used in windmill farms to generate electricity.

questions.q: Design a simple activity, different from the ones in the book, to help a younger student understand that wind is simply moving air, using materials you might find at home.
questions.a: Sample: Cut small strips of tissue paper and tape them loosely to a straw or stick; wave the stick through the air or stand near a fan and let air blow past the strips -- the strips will flutter and move, showing that the moving air is pushing against them, even though the air itself cannot be seen.

questions.q: Consider: (I) Air is a mixture of several gases, with nitrogen as the largest component. (II) Air is a single, pure gas called oxygen. Which is or are correct?

questions.q: Explain why the chapter emphasises that we cannot survive without oxygen for even a few minutes, even though oxygen makes up only about 21% of air, much less than nitrogen's 78%.
questions.a: Even though oxygen is a smaller percentage of air than nitrogen, the human body specifically needs oxygen to carry out its life processes; a gas's importance for survival depends on what the body actually uses, not simply on how large a percentage of air it makes up.
s: Notes that oxygen, despite being a smaller percentage, is the gas the body specifically needs
Explains that importance for survival is not the same as abundance/percentage

questions.q: A friend argues, 'Since nitrogen makes up 78% of air, it must be the most important gas for our survival.' Evaluate this claim using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: This claim is not correct. Abundance in air does not automatically make a gas the most important one for survival.
s: States the claim is incorrect
Correctly identifies oxygen, not nitrogen, as what the body needs for survival

s: Correctly conveys air as a mixture, not a single gas
Correctly names nitrogen as the larger component and oxygen as smaller

concepts.name: Water: uses, scarcity, conservation and rainwater harvesting
concepts.description: Most of Earth's water is saline; usable freshwater is limited, making conservation, avoiding pollution, and rainwater harvesting important.
concepts.idea: Water is essential for daily activities, but freshwater fit for these uses is only a small fraction of Earth's water, since most is saline ocean/sea water.
concepts.rule: Freshwater sources (ice, snow, rivers, lakes, groundwater) are often not easily accessible; conserving water is necessary since usable freshwater is limited and unevenly available.
concepts.example: Traditional stepwells such as bawadis and vavs store rainwater and seepage for later use; turning off taps when not in use and fixing leaks reduce water wastage.

concepts.name: Energy from the Sun
concepts.description: The Sun is Earth's main energy source, powering plant food-making directly and reaching animals and humans indirectly, plus direct/converted human uses.
concepts.idea: The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth; plants use sunlight to make food, and this energy passes to animals that eat plants, and further along the food chain.
concepts.rule: Sunlight can be used directly for heat and light, or converted into other useful forms such as electricity via solar panels, or used in solar cookers and solar water heaters.
concepts.example: A cow standing in the sun is not itself gaining energy from sunlight, but a cow eating grass IS ultimately getting energy from the Sun; drying chillies or mangoes in the sun uses the Sun's heat directly.

concepts.name: Forests, soil, rocks and minerals
concepts.description: Forests support biodiversity and protect soil, which forms slowly from rock disintegration; rocks contain minerals from which metals are extracted.
concepts.idea: Forests are large areas of dense plant growth that support biodiversity; soil forms over long periods from rock disintegration, and rocks contain minerals used to extract metals.
concepts.rule: Deforestation reduces forest cover, which takes many years to regrow; decaying leaves enrich soil with nutrients and earthworms loosen soil, while roots hold soil in place against erosion.
concepts.example: The Chipko movement in Uttarakhand saw villagers hug trees to stop them being felled; mobile phones contain about a dozen minerals, including gold, silver, copper and cobalt, extracted from rocks.

concepts.name: Fossil fuels
concepts.description: Petroleum, natural gas and coal are fossil fuels formed over millions of years from buried remains; they are limited and their burning causes air pollution.
concepts.idea: Fossil fuels -- petroleum, natural gas and coal -- are formed from the remains of microorganisms and plants buried deep underground over millions of years.
concepts.rule: Fossil fuels are limited and will run out if overused; burning them produces smoke and carbon dioxide, so alternatives like walking, cycling, public transport and cleaner fuels help conserve them and reduce pollution.
concepts.example: Petrol and diesel, the two most widely used vehicle fuels, both come from petroleum; coal is mainly used for electricity; natural gas is used for cooking, electricity and as CNG for vehicles.

concepts.name: Renewable and non-renewable resources; natural versus human-made resources
concepts.description: Natural resources split into renewable (quickly replenished, e.g. air, water, forests) and non-renewable (slow to form, e.g. minerals, soil, rocks, fossil fuels); human-made resources are manufactured by people.
concepts.idea: Resources provided by nature are natural resources; those made by humans using natural resources are human-made resources. Natural resources are classified as renewable or non-renewable.
concepts.rule: Renewable resources can be used more freely since nature restores them relatively quickly, but should still be used judiciously; non-renewable resources must be conserved carefully since they cannot be replaced within a human timescale.
concepts.example: Air, water and forests are renewable; coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals, soil and rocks are classified as non-renewable in this chapter, since they take a very long time to form.

questions.q: Resources provided by nature are called ____ resources.

questions.q: A classmate says, 'Non-renewable resources are always more valuable than renewable ones, since they can't be replaced.' Do you agree? Justify your answer using ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: I disagree with the statement as a general rule. While non-renewable resources do need careful conservation because they cannot be quickly replaced, renewable resources like air and water are absolutely essential for survival too, and can also become scarce or unusable if wasted, polluted or overused faster than nature can replenish them. Value depends on how essential and how threatened a resource is, not simply on whether it is renewable.
s: States disagreement or a nuanced response, not a flat agreement
Notes that renewable resources are still essential and can be threatened by overuse/pollution
Gives a reasoned basis for what actually determines a resource's importance
